hook: The painter of The Birth of Venus, favourite of the Medici.

pages.x: Alessandro Filipepi was born in Florence around 1445, the youngest son of a tanner. His nickname, Botticelli, "little barrel", came from his plump elder brother. He trained as a goldsmith, then with the painter Fra Filippo Lippi.

He became a favourite of the Medici, the banking family who ran Florence. He painted members of the family as the three kings in The Adoration of the Magi, and put himself in too, at the edge in a yellow cloak, looking out at us.
Around 1480 he painted Primavera, "Spring": Venus in an orange grove, the Three Graces dancing, Flora scattering flowers. Botanists have counted about 500 plants in it, of nearly 200 kinds.
In 1481 the pope called him to Rome with other leading painters to decorate the walls of his new Sistine Chapel, a quarter of a century before Michelangelo painted its ceiling.

His most famous picture shows the goddess Venus, newly born from the sea, drifting ashore on a scallop shell, blown by the winds. It was one of the first large paintings since ancient times of a goddess from the old myths.

In the 1490s the fiery preacher Savonarola turned Florence against luxury. Crowds threw mirrors, cards, fine clothes and paintings onto a great bonfire. A story says Botticelli threw in some of his own pictures. His late work grew darker and more religious.
Tastes changed, and he died poor in 1510, almost forgotten. For three centuries his paintings were ignored, until Victorian artists in England rediscovered him.
Botticelli's Venus and Primavera are among the best-loved paintings in the world, and his graceful figures still sum up the dreamy beauty of the early Renaissance.
